source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: An LLM can act as a black-box optimizer by seeing past solutions with scores in the prompt. On small TSPs it finds the optimum. Quality drops fast as the problem grows.
numbers: TSP, 5 random instances per size. n=10: all three LLMs 0.0% gap. n=15: text-bison 4.4%, gpt-3.5 1.2%, gpt-4 0.2%. n=20: 30.4%, 4.4%, 1.4%. n=50: 219.8%, 133.0%, 11.0% vs farthest insertion 9.8%.
limits: Only 5 instances per size. n=50 no LLM found the optimum. Authors say it is not meant to beat specialist solvers.
agent_relevance: A scored-history prompt works for small selection problems. For wide spaces the agent should not trust the LLM alone to pick from many candidates; pair it with a cheap heuristic or exact check.
quote: the farthest insertion heuristic starts to outperform all LLMs in the optimality gap

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: Model strength matters a lot. gpt-4 reached the optimum about 4x faster than the weaker LLMs on small TSPs.
numbers: n=10 steps to optimum: text-bison 40.4, gpt-3.5 46.8, gpt-4 9.6 (5 of 5 instances each). n=15 successes: text-bison 0/5, gpt-3.5 4/5, gpt-4 4/5.
limits: Single paper, three models, tiny instance count.
agent_relevance: Selection quality is model-dependent. Use the strongest model for the S7 select step and keep a cheap fallback.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: Sampling temperature acts as the explore-exploit dial. Default 1.0 gave the best prompt optimization; 0.0 and 0.5 lacked exploration, high values were noisier.
numbers: Ablation over optimizer temperatures {0.0,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}; 1.0 best. Optimized prompts beat human prompts by up to 8% on GSM8K and up to 50% on Big-Bench Hard tasks.
limits: Prompt-optimization task, not engineering design. Scorer and optimizer were PaLM-family models.
agent_relevance: Supports a diverse-first, then narrow, schedule for candidate generation and selection.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: Authors list failure modes: context length limits large problems, and bumpy landscapes make the LLM propose wrong directions, so search stalls halfway.
numbers: Linear regression and TSP failure cases described in appendix A.
limits: Qualitative; no failure rate given.
agent_relevance: Expect stall on rugged trade-off landscapes. Add a restart or an independent check when scores stop improving.
quote: the optimization landscape of some objective functions are too bumpy for the LLM to propose a correct descending direction

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Evolutionary Optimizers (LMEA)
finding: LLM-driven selection, crossover and mutation (LMEA) matched classic TSP heuristics up to 15 nodes, then fell behind at 20 and 25 nodes.
numbers: 8 test sets x 5 instances, GPT-3.5, N=16 and G=250 (4000 evaluations). Optimum found on 19 of 20 instances at n=10 and 15. rue-20 gap 3.94% vs farthest insertion 1.99%. rue-25 gap 18.72% vs 2.33%. clu-25 10.06% vs 2.10%.
limits: Instances up to 25 nodes only. Heuristic baselines are cheap and strong.
agent_relevance: The LLM works as a population search operator in small spaces. The edge disappears as the space grows, so S7 must not rely on LLM-only ranking for big option sets.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Evolutionary Optimizers (LMEA)
finding: Letting the LLM do the genetic operators beats just asking it for new solutions (OPRO) at every size tested.
limits: Both share one LLM (GPT-3.5) and the same budget; no human-effort comparison.
agent_relevance: Structured recombination of good options beats free generation. Select parents, then recombine, in the loop.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Evolutionary Optimizers (LMEA)
finding: A self-adaptation rule that raises LLM temperature when search stalls cut the gap by about two thirds.
numbers: rue-20 optimality gap: LMEA 3.94 +/- 1.54% vs without self-adaptation 11.82 +/- 2.21%.
limits: One test set (rue-20), 5 instances.
agent_relevance: Stall detection that increases exploration is a measured gain. Fits a re-open-the-space trigger in the loop.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Model for Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization (MOEA/D-LO)
finding: A general LLM used zero-shot as the search operator in MOEA/D is competitive with NSGA-II and MOEA/D on ZDT and UF benchmarks. Distilling it into a linear operator (MOEA/D-LO) keeps most of the gain.
numbers: 14 ZDT/UF problems, 30 runs each, hypervolume. Scoreboard of baseline vs LO (better/worse/equal): NSGA-II 2/11/1, MOEA/D 3/9/2, MOEA/D-DE 7/5/2. So LO beats NSGA-II on 11 and MOEA/D on 9 problems but loses to MOEA/D-DE on 7.
limits: Benchmark functions, not real design problems. Operator was learned from 14,000 LLM sample-response pairs.
agent_relevance: Shows the LLM is mostly a smooth linear recombiner, not magic reasoning. Do not over-credit LLM judgement in trade-off search.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Model for Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization (MOEA/D-LO)
finding: The best method depends on the problem. MOEA/D-DE wins the hard UF problems; NSGA-II wins some; the LLM-derived operator is robust but rarely best.
numbers: UF1 HV: DE 0.720, LO 0.656, NSGA-II 0.609, MOEA/D 0.553. UF3: DE 0.711, LO 0.498. ZDT4: DE collapsed to 0.301 (std 0.27) vs LO 0.721.
limits: 30 runs each; large std on UF problems.
agent_relevance: No single selector dominates. Report robustness across problems, not one win. Keep more than one search method in the toolkit.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models to Enhance Bayesian Optimization (LLAMBO)
finding: Adding an LLM to Bayesian optimization (zero-shot warm start, in-context surrogate, candidate sampler) gave the best tuning results, mostly early in the search when few observations exist.
numbers: 74 tasks (Bayesmark 25, HPOBench 24, plus 30 private/synthetic tasks to test memorization). 5 seeds, 25 trials, GPT-3.5. LLAMBO best average regret on both public and private/synthetic sets.
limits: Hyperparameter tuning only, low-dimensional. LLM inference costs far more compute than classic BO.
agent_relevance: Prior knowledge is most useful when evidence is thin. For first-pass option ranking the LLM is a good prior; later let observed scores dominate.
quote: excels in earlier stages of the search, when fewer observations are available

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models to Enhance Bayesian Optimization (LLAMBO)
finding: Warm-start points proposed by the LLM were less diverse than random ones (lower generalized variance), yet still helped search.
numbers: Generalized variance of LLM warm-start points lower than random init; better regret at the start. Memorization control used 3 proprietary and 2 synthetic datasets.
limits: Only a few control datasets; diversity loss is a risk.
agent_relevance: LLM proposals cluster. Force a diversity step before selecting, so the option set is not a family of near-copies.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Standard Gaussian Process is All You Need for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization
finding: A long-held belief that plain BO fails in high dimensions is mostly an artifact of the kernel and its initialization. With a Matern kernel or robust length-scale init, standard BO matches or beats methods built for high dimensions.
numbers: 12 benchmarks, compared with 9 high-dimensional BO methods. On Hartmann6 and Rosenbrock with initial length scale 0.5, Matern training failed from d=400 vs d=200 for the SE kernel. With init 1.0, Matern worked for all d tested (up to 600), SE failed from d=400.
limits: Mostly synthetic benchmarks; it challenges prior consensus and is itself not yet widely replicated.
agent_relevance: A famous negative result about a search method may hold only for a default setting. Check implementation details before dismissing an option.
quote: using Matern kernels enables standard BO to consistently achieve top-tier results

source: Liu et al. (2024) Evolution of Heuristics (EoH)
finding: Evolving both the idea (a thought in words) and the code beats evolving code alone and uses about 500x fewer LLM queries than FunSearch on online bin packing.
numbers: Fitness 0.962 to 0.993 in 20 generations, 2,000 queries, vs about 1 million for FunSearch. Excess bins on 1k C500: EoH 2.13%, best fit 4.50%, FunSearch 6.75%.
limits: FunSearch is better on some large sets (10k C100: 0.33% vs EoH 0.61%; 5k C100 tied at 0.80%). FunSearch comparison numbers are as reported in this paper.
agent_relevance: Natural-language reasons for why an option works help search. Write a short rationale per candidate before selecting.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Evolution of Heuristics (EoH)
finding: Generalization is uneven: FunSearch found a heuristic that worked in-distribution but lost to hand-made rules out of distribution.
numbers: 1k items, capacity 500 (shifted from training): FunSearch 6.75% excess vs first fit 4.97% and best fit 4.50%; EoH 2.13%.
limits: Single benchmark family (Weibull online bin packing).
agent_relevance: Selected options can overfit the evaluation distribution. Test the chosen option on a shifted case before committing.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Evolution of Heuristics (EoH)
finding: On flow-shop scheduling, EoH-made heuristics beat standard hand-made ones by a wide margin.
numbers: Flow shop relative makespan (%, lower is better), first Taillard sets: EoH 0.30, 0.10, 0.19, 0.60, 0.14 vs NEH 4.05, 3.06, 3.47, 5.48, 2.07.
limits: Values read from the paper table in text extraction; some columns garbled.
agent_relevance: LLM-guided search over methods can beat fixed rules on well-defined scored tasks.

source: Fu et al. (2023) GPT4AIGChip: AI accelerator design automation via LLMs
finding: Plain LLMs struggle in hardware design spaces: long dependencies in templates and rare languages hurt. The authors fix this by decoupling the template and adding demos.
numbers: GPT-4 Pass@100 42% vs CodeGen 0% without fine-tuning and 31% with. Pass@10 rose 10% to 30% to 60% as knowledge and demos were added.
limits: Code generation success, not Pareto quality. Hardware-specific.
agent_relevance: LLMs need worked examples to explore a technical space. In-prompt demos are a cheap booster to apply before a select step.

source: Fu et al. (2023) GPT4AIGChip: AI accelerator design automation via LLMs
finding: Generated accelerators beat a hand-designed baseline in latency on all six networks tested.
numbers: Latency reduction of 2.0% to 16.0% over CHaiDNN across six networks and two resolutions.
limits: Single hand-designed baseline; low end of the gain is small.
agent_relevance: Real design-space gains from LLM search exist but are modest and need a verifier in the loop.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) LUMINA: LLM-guided GPU architecture exploration
finding: An LLM with sensitivity-based bottleneck rules found 6 designs better than an A100 in only 20 steps in a 4.7 million point space, with 32.9% higher Pareto hypervolume and 17.5x sample efficiency than ML baselines.
numbers: Compared with ACO, random walk, BO, GA, grid search over 1,000 samples and several trials. BO ranked fourth overall; GA and grid search consistently failed to find high-quality designs; ACO best-to-worst PHV ratio 1.82x.
limits: Own simulator (LLMCompass, within 10% of hardware); GPT-3 inference workload only; benchmark built by the same authors.
agent_relevance: Bottleneck-first reasoning narrows the space fast. Locate the dominant limit, change one thing, re-check.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) LUMINA: LLM-guided GPU architecture exploration
finding: Off-the-shelf open LLMs are weak at architecture reasoning until failure patterns are written down as rules. Added guidance raised accuracy on every task.
numbers: Qwen3-80B accuracy default to enhanced: bottleneck 0.73 to 0.80; performance and area prediction 0.59 to 0.82; parameter tuning 0.40 to 0.63. Benchmark: 308, 127 and 30 questions.
limits: Small benchmark (30 tuning questions); rules were hand-written after seeing the errors, so partly tuned to the test.
agent_relevance: Self-made checklists from observed failures lift accuracy. Matches the schema's guardrail idea.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) LUMINA: LLM-guided GPU architecture exploration
finding: Two recurring LLM errors: changing many non-critical parameters at once, and computing deltas from the wrong baseline. Forcing one change at a time fixed them.
numbers: Rule added: adjust only the least critical resource when mitigating the dominant stall; models also ignored negative effects of bigger systolic arrays.
limits: Qualitative error analysis on three open models.
agent_relevance: One-change-at-a-time discipline in selection and tuning steps.

source: LLM-Driven Evolutionary Generation of Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization Algorithms (LLaMEA, 2026)
finding: LLM-evolved MOBO algorithms matched the state-of-the-art qParEGO on accuracy at about 60x lower wall-clock time, but a Friedman test put them in the same top group, so the accuracy gain is not clearly significant overall.
numbers: About 900 algorithms from 9 evolutionary runs, 12 synthetic problems, budget 400 evaluations, 5 repeats. Mean normalized hypervolume 0.971 (MOEAD-EI Hybrid) vs 0.869 (qParEGO) vs 0.691 (NSGA-II) vs 0.600 (random). Significantly better than qParEGO on 7 of 12 problems and never worse. Friedman chi2 = 49.91, p = 4.3e-8; mean ranks 1.83 vs 2.58.
limits: Selected on the same synthetic suite it is tested on; Gemini-2.5-flash only; LLM backbone and prompt not varied.
agent_relevance: A sound HV gain can still sit inside one equivalence group. Report significance and cost, and prefer speed when accuracy ties.

source: LLM-Driven Evolutionary Generation of Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization Algorithms (LLaMEA, 2026)
finding: Transfer to unseen real engineering problems held, but the ranking test was underpowered. NSGA-II without any surrogate stayed competitive.
numbers: 3 real-world problems: best generated 0.985 vs qParEGO 0.971, significantly better on 2 of 3, at about 3.4x lower cost; NSGA-II 0.849; MOEAD-EI Hybrid 0.926 (third).
limits: Only three unconstrained problems; authors call the rank-based test underpowered.
agent_relevance: A plain population method is a strong baseline in small, multi-peaked spaces. Keep it as the control in any option comparison.

source: LLM-Driven Evolutionary Generation of Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization Algorithms (LLaMEA, 2026)
finding: Generated code can quietly become deterministic: without an explicit instruction the LLM may fix the random seed, which removes the stochasticity the method needs.
numbers: Described as an unexpected hazard in the discussion; no rate given.
limits: Single report, qualitative.
agent_relevance: Check that generated search routines keep randomness. A fixed seed makes repeated trials meaningless.
quote: absent an explicit instruction, an LLM may generate deterministic heuristics

source: Ping et al. (2026) POET: Power-Oriented Evolutionary Tuning for LLM-based RTL PPA optimization
finding: Combining LLM mutation with NSGA-II style non-dominated sorting, power-first ranking inside each level, and a verified testbench gave full functional correctness and best power on all 40 designs.
numbers: RTL-OPT benchmark, 40 designs. Functional correctness 40/40 (100%) vs 29/40 (72.5%) I/O prompting, 33/40 (82.5%) chain-of-thought, 36/40 (90.0%) a third baseline. Best power 40/40, best area 29 (72.5%), best delay 27 (67.5%). Raw DeepSeek-R1 introduces errors in over 25% of attempts.
limits: One benchmark; the ablation table was only skimmed. Baseline names taken from the text.
agent_relevance: Do not scalarize trade-offs with hand weights. Rank by Pareto level first, then by the preferred objective; check correctness with a deterministic oracle.

source: Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, Meyarivan (2002) A fast and elitist multiobjective genetic algorithm: NSGA-II
finding: Founding method for Pareto selection. NSGA-II sorts solutions into non-dominated fronts and breaks ties by crowding distance.
numbers: Not opened this session. From memory: cost O(MN^2) per generation vs O(MN^3) for the first NSGA.
limits: Not read here; recheck before citing.
agent_relevance: Basis of the select step used by POET and the MOBO baselines above.

source: Ishibuchi, Tsukamoto, Nojima (2008) Evolutionary many-objective optimization: a short review
finding: Pareto dominance loses selection pressure as objectives grow beyond about four, so NSGA-II-type methods stall on many-objective problems.
numbers: Not opened this session.
limits: Not read here; recheck before citing.
agent_relevance: Boundary: with many criteria, Pareto sorting alone does not choose. S7 needs an extra tie-break rule.

source: Wolpert and Macready (1997) No free lunch theorems for optimization
finding: Averaged over all problems, no search algorithm beats another, so a method's edge comes from fit to the problem class.
numbers: Not opened this session.
limits: Theoretical; real problem classes are not uniform.
agent_relevance: Supports reporting results per problem class and keeping a portfolio of search styles, as the results above show.
